DartPoints markets the building as engineered to withstand EF-5 tornadoes, the most severe rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale, a notable resilience feature given Indiana's exposure to severe Midwest storm systems. profile.reading:
DartPoints operates a colocation facility at 8480 Palmetto Commerce Parkway in Ladson, South Carolina, inside Palmetto Commerce Park, a large industrial and logistics park in the tri county area where Charleston, Berkeley, and Dorchester counties meet, with DartPoints' own materials placing this specific parcel in Charleston County. The facility began as Immedion, a Southeastern colocation operator that built the North Charleston area site as part of a small regional footprint, before DartPoints acquired Immedion in 2021 in a deal the company said tripled its total data center footprint to eight facilities across seven markets in Ohio, Indiana, North Carolina, and South Carolina. DartPoints itself grew out of earlier rural and secondary market fiber and colocation providers and has positioned itself as a builder of infrastructure in markets larger operators tend to skip.

DartPoints' own current specification page for this site, referenced internally as CHS01, states a 15,000 square foot data hall, 90 tons of N plus 1 redundant cooling, seven on site network providers, and two power figures worth keeping separate rather than treating as one number, 1.3 megawatts of utility power delivered to the building, and a critical IT load capacity of 100 kilowatts. That gap between utility feed and actual IT load is common in colocation facilities built with room to grow, and it means this site's IT capacity today is a small fraction of the power physically available to it. No diesel standby generator rating or onsite generation figure specific to this address was found in operator materials reviewed for this entry.

Because Palmetto Commerce Park sits at the edge of several utility territories in the Charleston area, this research could not confirm with certainty whether the parcel is served by Dominion Energy South Carolina or by Berkeley Electric Cooperative, both of which serve parts of the surrounding tri county region, and no county assessor record was pulled to confirm parcel ownership, year built, or improved square footage separate from the operator's stated data hall size. What is documented is DartPoints' 2021 acquisition of the Immedion asset, the facility's role in a wider seven market footprint, and its stated cooling and power design as published on the operator's own site. What remains undocumented locally is any zoning case, incentive agreement, or utility interconnection filing specific to this parcel, and the exact year the building was originally constructed under Immedion.

profile.reading:
DartPoints operates CAE01 in Suite 180 at 1000 Catawba Street in Columbia, South Carolina, and the most useful thing to know about it is the building it sits inside. That address is the USC Columbia Innovation Center, run by SCRA, the South Carolina Research Authority, which is a public non profit corporation chartered by the State of South Carolina in 1983. SCRA describes the building as 66,000 square feet with 8,000 square feet of its own offices, marketed to technology businesses and start ups near the University of South Carolina's Innovista research district and the state house. The Columbia Star reported its grand opening on 19 August 2010, calling it a 74,000 square foot building designed by Garvin Design Group and built by Mashburn Construction, so the state agency's current listing and the 2010 press account differ on gross area. SCRA's own tenant page makes no mention of a data centre or colocation at all. This facility is therefore a colocation suite leased inside a state chartered innovation centre, not a purpose built data centre, and that single fact explains almost everything about its scale.

The operator arrived by acquisition rather than construction. The site came from Immedion, a Greenville founded colocation provider established in 2007 with eight data centres across seven markets, which DartPoints announced it was buying on 16 March 2021. DartPoints is a Dallas based operator concentrating on smaller markets on the argument that they deserve the same infrastructure as the large metros. NOVA Infrastructure took majority control on 30 April 2025 with more than 250 million dollars in committed capital including a senior secured facility from Orion Infrastructure Capital, with Astra Capital Management retaining a minority position, at a point when DartPoints described 11 data centres across 10 markets in South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Indiana and Louisiana and more than 900 enterprise customers. On 27 May 2026 the company bought a campus in Lexington, Kentucky of roughly 343,000 square feet on 29.5 acres with about 81,000 square feet of existing raised floor, a first phase path to 20 to 30 megawatts and long term potential to 70 megawatts at up to 200 kilowatts per rack. That is the direction of the business, and it is the clearest way to see how small the Columbia suite is by comparison.

The power numbers are worth reading slowly, because this row is a clean illustration of why the two figures must never be conflated. DartPoints publishes utility power of 2 megawatts and a critical IT load of 110 kilowatts for this site, alongside 15,000 square feet of raised floor, an 8,200 square foot data hall, 120 tons of cooling in N plus 1, ten on site network providers and five diverse fibre entries. Its South Carolina market page repeats the same 110 kilowatt critical IT load but gives utility power as 2.5 megawatts, so the two operator pages disagree about the electrical service and agree about the load. The gap between the two kinds of number is instructive rather than embarrassing. The service into a mixed use office building is roughly eighteen times the protected IT load in the suite, which is precisely why a utility service rating must never be reprinted as capacity. The published IT load works out at about thirteen watts per square foot of data hall, a density consistent with legacy enterprise and interconnection racks rather than anything resembling modern accelerated computing. No standby diesel rating and no on site generation figure is published for this site. The market page also claims SOC 2 Type II and Uptime Institute Tier III Design, which the individual facility page does not corroborate, so neither is asserted here.

South Carolina's public argument about data centres has been loud through 2026, and almost none of it touches a site this size. Counties have been enacting moratoriums one after another, Spartanburg for a year from 19 July 2026, Greenwood for twelve months from late June, Colleton for six months following a first vote in May, with Chesterfield and Newberry acting in early June, the last of those after rejecting the sale of county industrial park land to a data centre developer. No comparable action by Richland County or the City of Columbia appeared in the public record reviewed for this entry, and that absence is reported as an absence rather than as a finding that none exists. At state level, two Senate bills in the 2025 to 2026 session, one placing data centre oversight in the Department of Environmental Services and one placing it with the Public Service Commission, would have created state permitting with review periods scaled to project size, and neither reached a floor vote. A separate House bill on data centre utility costs was filed in the same session. Dominion Energy told reporters in March 2026 that it had nine potential data centres in its South Carolina pipeline, all of them proposed by speculative developers rather than named end users, while Duke Energy reported 40 operating data centres across the Carolinas drawing about 470 megawatts in total, only three of them above 50 megawatts. A 110 kilowatt suite inside a state innovation centre is invisible in that debate, and saying so is more useful than implying otherwise.

What is not known is when the suite was fitted out, which utility serves the building, whether the 15,000 square foot raised floor figure includes support space outside the 8,200 square foot hall, which of the two published utility service figures is current, what backup generation the suite has, and who the tenants are.

The facility also became the first South Carolina point of presence for Megaport, a global network-as-a-service provider, per a partnership covered by GSA Business Report, a South Carolina trade publication, around July 2025. DartPoints' South Carolina market-overview page describes this and its sibling South Carolina sites as SOC 2 Type II and Uptime Institute Tier III Design certified, though the individual facility page uses only general "AICPA SOC-compliant" language without independently corroborating those specific certifications, a discrepancy noted honestly rather than resolved. As is standard industry practice, tenant identities are not publicly disclosed.

DartPoints markets itself company-wide as serving more than 900 enterprise customers, including universities, hospital systems, and Fortune 500 companies, and has been recognized on the Inc. 5000 list of fastest-growing private US companies in multiple recent years.

profile.reading:
DartPoints operates SPA01 at 5700 North Blackstock Road in Spartanburg, South Carolina, close to where Interstates 26 and 85 meet north of the city centre. It is a single enterprise colocation building rather than a campus, and it exists in DartPoints' portfolio because the company bought its way into the market rather than building here. The facility came from Immedion, a Greenville headquartered colocation provider founded in 2007 that ran eight data centres across seven markets, and which DartPoints announced it was acquiring on 16 March 2021.

DartPoints itself is a Dallas based operator that deliberately targets what it calls Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets, on the argument that smaller cities deserve the same infrastructure as the large metros. NOVA Infrastructure, a middle market North American infrastructure investor founded in 2018, took majority control on 30 April 2025 with more than 250 million dollars of committed capital, including a senior secured credit facility from Orion Infrastructure Capital, while Astra Capital Management retained a minority stake. At that point DartPoints described 11 data centres across 10 markets in South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Indiana and Louisiana, serving more than 900 enterprise customers including universities, hospital systems and Fortune 500 companies. The company has since moved upmarket. On 27 May 2026 it acquired a campus in Lexington, Kentucky of roughly 343,000 square feet on 29.5 acres with about 81,000 square feet of existing raised floor, describing a first phase path to 20 to 30 megawatts and long term expansion potential to 70 megawatts at up to 200 kilowatts per rack. Reading Spartanburg next to Lexington is the fastest way to understand what this building is and is not.

On power, DartPoints is unusually explicit, which is worth noting because most operators are not. The SPA01 page prints utility power of 1.6 megawatts and a critical IT load of 0.8 megawatts as separate labelled figures, alongside 21,400 square feet of raised floor, 200 tons of cooling, five on site network providers, a 99.999 percent uptime commitment and AICPA SOC compliance. Because the operator itself labels the 0.8 megawatt figure as IT load, it is stored as IT capacity here. The 1.6 megawatt figure is the electrical service the building can draw and is stored separately as utility power, never as capacity. The company's South Carolina market page then disagrees with its own facility page in two places, giving a 7,000 square foot data hall and 1.3 megawatts of utility power, while repeating the identical 0.8 megawatt critical IT load. The disagreement is therefore about floor area and about utility service, not about IT load, and both figures are left standing rather than one being quietly preferred. That market page also asserts SOC 2 Type II and Uptime Institute Tier III Design for the site, neither of which the facility page corroborates, so neither is treated here as confirmed. No standby diesel rating and no on site generation figure is published for this building at all.

The local record in Spartanburg County is now substantial, though almost none of it concerns this facility. On 19 July 2026 the county council voted unanimously for a one year moratorium on new data centre applications, extendable by further vote, covering pending applications that have not been finalised and exempting projects already approved, so an operating building such as this one is untouched. The trigger was an application for a site that had run bitcoin mining for years. The project actually driving the argument sits elsewhere in the county, where Valara Holdings, a subsidiary of NorthMark Strategies, is converting the former Kohler kitchen and bath plant on roughly 300 acres south east of the city into a computing centre described as a 2.8 billion dollar investment with 27 projected jobs. It was first approved at about 50 megawatts and amended in March 2026 to 450 megawatts, with on site generation of 24 natural gas generators of 2,000 kilowatts each plus a further request to add five 17 megawatt and six 54 megawatt combustion turbines. On 27 August 2026 the South Carolina Public Service Commission ruled unanimously, with Commissioner David Britt recused, that because the plant will not export power to the grid for public use it falls outside the state Utility Siting Act and its public review requirements. A separate lawsuit filed on 6 July 2026 challenges the county's classification of the permitting as minor development. For wider scale, Duke Energy told reporters in March 2026 that its data centre backlog across the Carolinas had fallen from more than 100 requests to fewer than five, that it serves 40 operating data centres of which only three exceed 50 megawatts, and that together they draw about 470 megawatts, roughly one percent of its Carolinas production. Two South Carolina Senate bills in the 2025 to 2026 session that would have created state level data centre permitting did not reach a floor vote.

What is not known about SPA01 is the year the building was fitted out as a data centre, which utility serves it, whether the raised floor is 21,400 or 7,000 square feet, what its backup generation rating is, and who its tenants are. DartPoints publishes none of that, and no local filing was found that would resolve it, because a building of this size in South Carolina generates no rezoning fight and therefore no public record.

reading:
DartPoints is a privately held colocation operator headquartered at 1601 Elm Street, Suite 3650, Dallas, Texas, founded in the early 2000s. NOVA Infrastructure made a strategic growth investment in the company in 2025.

The company positions itself explicitly around secondary markets, describing its mission as bringing enterprise-grade colocation, cloud, and managed infrastructure to communities outside the largest US metros, with an emphasis on AI-ready, high-density capacity supporting regional economic growth. Its operator site lists 11 facilities across Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, and South Carolina, naming Columbus, Indiana, Baton Rouge and Shreveport, Louisiana, Asheville, North Carolina, Cincinnati and Dublin, Ohio, and Columbia, Charleston, Greenville, and Spartanburg, South Carolina.

The registry here tracks 10 DartPoints facilities across four states, Indiana, Louisiana, Ohio, and South Carolina, closely matching the operator's own named markets, with North Carolina the one state named on the operator's site not reflected among this registry's current DartPoints rows. As an explicitly Tier 2/Tier 3-focused operator, DartPoints stands apart from the metro-core colocation model of Equinix and CoreSite and the hyperscaler campus model of AWS and Meta recorded elsewhere in this registry, representing smaller-market colocation demand rather than large-scale AI training capacity.
